claim: Auditory processing depends upon inhibitory signaling by interneurons, even at its earliest stages in the ventral cochlear nucleus (VCN).
source: Auditory processing depends upon inhibitory signaling by interneurons, even at its earliest stages in the ventral cochlear nucleus (VCN).
evidence: This is a general statement about auditory processing that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: To date only a single subtype of inhibitory neuron has been documented in the VCN, a projection neuron termed the D-stellate cell.
source: Remarkably, to date only a single subtype of inhibitory neuron has been documented in the VCN, a projection neuron termed the D-stellate cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior literature establishing the D-stellate cell as the only known inhibitory neuron type in VCN.

claim: A population of glycinergic cells in the VCN distinct from the D-stellate cell was revealed using a transgenic mouse line, optical clearing, and imaging techniques, combined with electrophysiological tools.
source: With the use of a transgenic mouse line, optical clearing, and imaging techniques, combined with electrophysiological tools, we revealed a population of glycinergic cells in the VCN distinct from the D-stellate cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript using multiple methodological approaches.

claim: The multipolar glycinergic cells were smaller in soma size and dendritic area than D-stellate cells.
source: These multipolar glycinergic cells were smaller in soma size and dendritic area, but over ten-fold more numerous than D-stellate cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The multipolar glycinergic cells were over ten-fold more numerous than D-stellate cells.
source: These multipolar glycinergic cells were smaller in soma size and dendritic area, but over ten-fold more numerous than D-stellate cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell counting data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The small glycinergic cells were activated by auditory nerve and T-stellate cells.
source: They were activated by auditory nerve and T-stellate cells, and made local inhibitory synaptic contacts on principal cells of the VCN.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing synaptic responses.

claim: The small glycinergic cells made local inhibitory synaptic contacts on principal cells of the VCN.
source: They were activated by auditory nerve and T-stellate cells, and made local inhibitory synaptic contacts on principal cells of the VCN.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing inhibitory postsynaptic currents in principal cells.

claim: L-stellate cells likely play a significant role in frequency-specific processing of acoustic signals given their abundance, narrow dendritic fields and axonal projections.
source: Given their abundance, combined with their narrow dendritic fields and axonal projections, it is likely that these neurons, here termed L-stellate cells, play a significant role in frequency-specific processing of acoustic signals.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the morphological and numerical characteristics of L-stellate cells.

claim: In the VCN, auditory nerve afferents make synapses onto multiple subtypes of excitatory neurons, setting up parallel streams of processing.
source: In the ventral cochlear nucleus (VCN), auditory nerve (AN) afferents make synapses onto multiple subtypes of excitatory neurons, setting up parallel streams of processing that are used by higher centers for processing auditory cues for sound intensity, frequency, and localization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VCN circuitry.

claim: Early-level activity of excitatory neurons in the VCN is sculpted and stabilized by inhibitory neurons, which use the transmitter glycine.
source: This early-level activity of excitatory neurons is sculpted and stabilized by inhibitory neurons, which use the transmitter glycine (Altschuler et al., 1986; Wenthold et al., 1986; Wu and Oertel, 1986; Kolston et al., 1992; Ferragamo et al., 1998a; Chanda and Xu-Friedman, 2010; Xie and Manis, 2013b; Xie and Manis, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Glycinergic inputs onto excitatory bushy and T-stellate cells enhance acoustic tuning properties and temporal precision.
source: For example, glycinergic inputs onto excitatory bushy and T-stellate (i.e., Trapezoid body projecting) cells enhance acoustic tuning properties and temporal precision, and stabilize neuronal firing responses to acoustic inputs (Caspary et al., 1994; Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2002; Gai and Carney, 2008; Keine and Rübsamen, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Glycinergic inputs stabilize neuronal firing responses to acoustic inputs.
source: For example, glycinergic inputs onto excitatory bushy and T-stellate (i.e., Trapezoid body projecting) cells enhance acoustic tuning properties and temporal precision, and stabilize neuronal firing responses to acoustic inputs (Caspary et al., 1994; Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2002; Gai and Carney, 2008; Keine and Rübsamen, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The sources of inhibitory glycinergic inputs onto the principal cells in the VCN are not well understood.
source: However, the sources of these inhibitory glycinergic inputs onto the principal cells in the VCN are not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: D-stellate cells are called radiate multipolar cells.
source: Within the VCN, only a single glycinergic inhibitory cell type, called the D-stellate or radiate multipolar cell, has been described (Oertel, 1983; Sento and Ryugo, 1989; Oertel et al., 1990; Doucet and Ryugo, 1997; Oertel et al., 2011; Xie and Manis, 2014).
evidence: This is established nomenclature supported by citations.

claim: D-stellate cells are a small population of neurons.
source: D-stellate (i.e., Dorsal projecting) cells are a small population of neurons (Doucet and Ryugo, 1997; Doucet et al., 1999) that send their axons to the ipsilateral dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN) (Smith and Rhode, 1989; Oertel et al., 2011; Campagnola and Manis, 2014) but also to sites as distant as the contralateral cochlear nucleus (CN) (Schofield and Cant, 1996b; Needham and Paolini, 2003; Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: D-stellate cells send their axons to the ipsilateral dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN).
source: D-stellate (i.e., Dorsal projecting) cells are a small population of neurons (Doucet and Ryugo, 1997; Doucet et al., 1999) that send their axons to the ipsilateral dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN) (Smith and Rhode, 1989; Oertel et al., 2011; Campagnola and Manis, 2014) but also to sites as distant as the contralateral cochlear nucleus (CN) (Schofield and Cant, 1996b; Needham and Paolini, 2003; Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: D-stellate cells project to the contralateral cochlear nucleus (CN).
source: D-stellate (i.e., Dorsal projecting) cells are a small population of neurons (Doucet and Ryugo, 1997; Doucet et al., 1999) that send their axons to the ipsilateral dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN) (Smith and Rhode, 1989; Oertel et al., 2011; Campagnola and Manis, 2014) but also to sites as distant as the contralateral cochlear nucleus (CN) (Schofield and Cant, 1996b; Needham and Paolini, 2003; Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: D-stellate cells provide broadband inhibition to their targets.
source: Importantly, D-stellate cells provide broadband inhibition to their targets, as their large dendritic arbors receive input from a broad frequency spectrum of auditory nerve fibers (ANFs) (Smith and Rhode, 1989; Oertel et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: D-stellate cells have large dendritic arbors that receive input from a broad frequency spectrum of auditory nerve fibers.
source: Importantly, D-stellate cells provide broadband inhibition to their targets, as their large dendritic arbors receive input from a broad frequency spectrum of auditory nerve fibers (ANFs) (Smith and Rhode, 1989; Oertel et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Tuberculoventral cells (also called vertical cells) are a source of inhibition in VCN and are projection neurons originating in the DCN.
source: Another source of inhibition in VCN is a projection neuron originating in the DCN, the tuberculoventral cells (also called vertical cells) (Wickesberg and Oertel, 1988; Wickesberg et al., 1991; Xie and Manis, 2013a; Campagnola and Manis, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: D-stellate and tuberculoventral cells do not fully account for the inhibition observed in VCN principal cells in vivo and in vitro.
source: Recent studies suggest that D-stellate and tuberculoventral cells do not fully account for the inhibition observed in VCN principal cells in vivo (Keine and Rübsamen, 2015) and in vitro (Campagnola and Manis, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: No local inhibitory interneuron has ever been described for VCN.
source: Indeed, no local inhibitory interneuron has ever been described for VCN, which is unlike most known brain regions.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Early anatomical studies suggested the presence of short axon cells in the VCN.
source: Early anatomical studies suggested the presence of short axon cells in the VCN (Lorente de Nó, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Previous histological studies reported the presence of small inhibitory neurons (glycinergic or possibly GABAergic) that are different from the D-stellate cells, but the identity of such neurons is unknown.
source: Furthermore, previous histological studies also reported the presence of small inhibitory neurons (glycinergic or possibly GABAergic) that are different from the D-stellate cells, but the identity of such neurons is unknown (Wenthold, 1987; Kolston et al., 1992; Doucet and Ryugo, 1997; Gleich and Vater, 1998; Doucet et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior histological studies.

claim: GlyT2-GFP transgenic mouse labels virtually all glycinergic neurons in the CN.
source: Here we comprehensively examined the diversity of inhibitory neurons in the VCN using a well-characterized transgenic mouse line, GlyT2-GFP, (Zeilhofer et al., 2005; Kuo et al., 2012; Moore and Trussell, 2017) which labels virtually all glycinergic neurons in the CN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior characterizations of the mouse line.

claim: A large population of inhibitory glycinergic cell types distinct from the D-stellate cell was discovered in the VCN.
source: With the use of this transgenic mouse, as well as optical tissue clearing, whole CN super-resolution microscopy, electrophysiological, and morphological tools, we discovered a large population of inhibitory glycinergic cell types distinct from the D-stellate cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using multiple techniques.

claim: The novel glycinergic neurons have a narrower dendritic field than D-stellate cells.
source: The novel glycinergic neurons, which have a narrower dendritic field than D-stellate cells, form the vast majority of inhibitory neurons in the VCN.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: The novel glycinergic neurons form the vast majority of inhibitory neurons in the VCN.
source: The novel glycinergic neurons, which have a narrower dendritic field than D-stellate cells, form the vast majority of inhibitory neurons in the VCN.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell counting data presented in the manuscript.

claim: L-stellate cells receive monosynaptic ANF inputs.
source: We show that these cells, which we have termed L-stellate cells, receive monosynaptic ANF inputs and polysynaptic inputs from axon collaterals of T-stellate cells, and in turn locally inhibit bushy and T-stellate cells in the VCN.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing short-latency EPSCs.

claim: L-stellate cells receive polysynaptic inputs from axon collaterals of T-stellate cells.
source: We show that these cells, which we have termed L-stellate cells, receive monosynaptic ANF inputs and polysynaptic inputs from axon collaterals of T-stellate cells, and in turn locally inhibit bushy and T-stellate cells in the VCN.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing delayed EPSCs that increase with carbachol.

claim: L-stellate cells locally inhibit bushy and T-stellate cells in the VCN.
source: We show that these cells, which we have termed L-stellate cells, receive monosynaptic ANF inputs and polysynaptic inputs from axon collaterals of T-stellate cells, and in turn locally inhibit bushy and T-stellate cells in the VCN.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing IPSCs in principal cells.

claim: The VCN has a rich diversity of glycinergic interneurons to provide maximum flexibility to control the excitability of projection neurons in the VCN.
source: Thus, the VCN has a rich diversity of glycinergic interneurons to provide maximum flexibility to control the excitability of projection neurons in the VCN.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: The neuronal glycine transporter, GlyT2, is a reliable marker of glycinergic cells.
source: The neuronal glycine transporter, GlyT2, is a reliable marker of glycinergic cells, and GFP is selectively expressed in >90% of glycinergic cells in the CN.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GlyT2 marker.

claim: GFP is selectively expressed in >90% of glycinergic cells in the CN in the GlyT2-GFP mouse.
source: The neuronal glycine transporter, GlyT2, is a reliable marker of glycinergic cells, and GFP is selectively expressed in >90% of glycinergic cells in the CN.
evidence: This claim is supported by characterization of the transgenic mouse line.

claim: A dense population of glycinergic cells was observed in the DCN.
source: Not surprisingly, we observed a dense population of glycinergic cells in the DCN as described in previous studies (Oertel and Wu, 1989; Zhang and Oertel, 1993b; Zhang and Oertel, 1993a; Kuo et al., 2012; Apostolides and Trussell, 2014).
evidence: This observation is supported by imaging data and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: Thick tracts of glycinergic fibers entered the dorsal part of VCN, presumably projections of the glycinergic tuberculoventral neurons (vertical cells) in the DCN.
source: Also apparent were thick tracts of glycinergic fibers that entered the dorsal part of VCN, presumably projections of the glycinergic tuberculoventral neurons (vertical cells) in the DCN (Figure 1A).
evidence: This observation is supported by imaging data and inference based on known anatomy.

claim: There was an obvious lack of glycinergic cells in the octopus cell region of the posterior VCN.
source: There was an obvious lack of glycinergic cells in the octopus cell region of the posterior VCN, consistent with previous studies (Wickesberg and Oertel, 1988; Wickesberg et al., 1991).
evidence: This observation is supported by imaging data and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: A large population of glycinergic cells was found distributed across the rest of the VCN.
source: However, we found a large population of glycinergic cells distributed across the rest of the VCN.
evidence: This observation is supported by imaging data.

claim: The high density of glycinergic cells throughout VCN was surprising, because D-stellate cells are thought to be sparse.
source: The high density of glycinergic cells throughout VCN was surprising, because D-stellate cells are thought to be sparse, and the only other known glycinergic cells are Golgi cells, which are present mainly in the granule cell layer overlying VCN (Ferragamo et al., 1998b; Irie et al., 2006; Yaeger and Trussell, 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging data in the context of prior knowledge.

claim: Golgi cells are present mainly in the granule cell layer overlying VCN.
source: The high density of glycinergic cells throughout VCN was surprising, because D-stellate cells are thought to be sparse, and the only other known glycinergic cells are Golgi cells, which are present mainly in the granule cell layer overlying VCN (Ferragamo et al., 1998b; Irie et al., 2006; Yaeger and Trussell, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The total count of glycinergic neurons in the VCN was 2706 ± 107 (n = 4 VCNs, three mice).
source: This counting procedure yielded a total of 2706 ± 107 glycinergic neurons in the VCN (n = 4 VCNs, three mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data.

claim: The soma volume distribution of glycinergic cells was positively skewed.
source: Next, we quantified the soma volumes of all glycinergic neurons using the 'surface function' in Imaris (Figure 2C,D), and found that the soma volume distribution was positively skewed (Figure 2E), such that the vast majority of the glycinergic cells had small somas, and a minority had large somas (Figure 2E, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of soma volumes shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The vast majority of the glycinergic cells had small somas, and a minority had large somas.
source: Next, we quantified the soma volumes of all glycinergic neurons using the 'surface function' in Imaris (Figure 2C,D), and found that the soma volume distribution was positively skewed (Figure 2E), such that the vast majority of the glycinergic cells had small somas, and a minority had large somas (Figure 2E, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of soma volumes shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The proportion of GFP expressing cells also positive for glycine was 93.44 ± 1.54%.
source: The proportion of GFP expressing cells also positive for glycine was 93.44 ± 1.54%, whereas the proportion of glycine-positive cells also expressing GFP was 99.5% (n = 442 cells, n = 3 VCNs, three mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: The proportion of glycine-positive cells also expressing GFP was 99.5%.
source: The proportion of GFP expressing cells also positive for glycine was 93.44 ± 1.54%, whereas the proportion of glycine-positive cells also expressing GFP was 99.5% (n = 442 cells, n = 3 VCNs, three mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data.

claim: RNA probes against the Slc6a5 gene (GlyT2) clearly reveal both large and small glycinergic cells types in VCN.
source: Interestingly, RNA probes against the Slc6a5 gene (GlyT2) also clearly reveal both large and small glycinergic cells types in VCN (https://mouse.brain-map.org/experiment/show/69874024).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to external RNA expression data.

claim: Large GFP-positive cells were clearly positive for tdTomato in the SST-Cre::Ai9::GlyT2-GFP mouse line.
source: In the resulting cross, large GFP-positive cells were clearly positive for tdTomato; given their size, these are candidate D-stellate cells, and this inference was confirmed by experiments described below on commissural projections.
evidence: This observation is supported by imaging data from the triple transgenic mouse.

claim: The large GFP and tdTomato double-positive cells are D-stellate cells.
source: In the resulting cross, large GFP-positive cells were clearly positive for tdTomato; given their size, these are candidate D-stellate cells, and this inference was confirmed by experiments described below on commissural projections.
evidence: This inference is based on cell size and confirmed by retrobead experiments.

claim: The majority of the GFP positive cells were tdTomato-negative and thus formed a size class distinct from the double-labeled cells presumed to be D-stellate cells.
source: However, closer examination revealed that the majority of the GFP positive cells were tdTomato-negative and thus formed a size class distinct from the double-labeled cells presumed to be D-stellate cells.
evidence: This observation is supported by imaging data from the triple transgenic mouse.

claim: There was a strong correlation between GFP and tdTomato expression in presumptive D-stellate cells.
source: There was a strong correlation between GFP and tdTomato expression in presumptive D-stellate cells (Figure 3B, top row).
evidence: This observation is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Smaller cells that were GFP positive were clearly tdTomato negative.
source: By contrast, smaller cells that were GFP positive were clearly tdTomato negative (Figure 3B, bottom row).
evidence: This observation is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The small glycinergic cells were molecularly distinct from the larger D-stellate cells in that only the latter expressed Cre in the SST-Cre mouse line.
source: Thus, the small glycinergic cells were molecularly distinct from the larger D-stellate cells in that only the latter expressed Cre in this mouse line.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the differential expression of tdTomato in the SST-Cre reporter line.

claim: Double-labeled cells were significantly larger than GFP-only cells (average soma volume, GFP only, 1826.6 ± 12.9 μm3 versus D-stellate cells, 4289.5 ± 98.3 μm3, n = 2 VCNs, two mice).
source: We found a broad distribution of soma size of double-labeled, D-stellate cells. This suggest that soma size alone is not a predictive indicator of cell class. However, we found that on average double-labeled cells were significantly larger than GFP-only cells (average soma volume, GFP only, 1826.6 ± 12.9 μm3 versus D-stellate cells, 4289.5 ± 98.3 μm3, n = 2 VCNs, two mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of soma volumes.

claim: Soma size alone is not a predictive indicator of cell class.
source: We found a broad distribution of soma size of double-labeled, D-stellate cells. This suggest that soma size alone is not a predictive indicator of cell class.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation of a broad distribution of soma sizes in D-stellate cells.

claim: The larger cell types composed only about 12% of all glycinergic neurons in VCN (GFP only, n = 3250 ± 55 versus D-stellate cells, n = 380 ± 9).
source: However, numerically, the larger cell types composed only about 12% of all glycinergic neurons in VCN (GFP only, n = 3250 ± 55 versus D-stellate cells, n = 380 ± 9) (Figure 4C, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data.

claim: D-stellate cell types and small glycinergic cell types are molecularly distinct populations of glycinergic interneurons in the VCN.
source: Our data thus indicate that D-stellate cell types and small glycinergic cell types are molecularly distinct populations of glycinergic interneurons in the VCN, and also shows that the small cells compose the vast majority of glycinergic neurons in the VCN.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the differential expression of SST-Cre and cell counting data.

claim: Large cells exhibited typical radiate morphology which have been described previously for D-stellate cells in the VCN.
source: Large cells exhibited typical radiate morphology which have been described previously for D-stellate cells in the VCN (Oertel et al., 1990; Campagnola and Manis, 2014; Xie and Manis, 2014) (n = 6) (Figure 5A), and henceforth will be referred to as D-stellate cells.
evidence: This observation is supported by morphological reconstructions and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: The small glycinergic cells had restricted axonal and dendritic arbors.
source: Unlike D-stellate cells, the small glycinergic cells had restricted axonal and dendritic arbors (n = 17) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This observation is supported by morphological reconstructions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The small glycinergic cells had significantly restricted branched processes compared with D-stellate cells (longest axis: D-stellate cells, 619.42 ± 45.78 μm versus small cells, 271.43 ± 26.27 μm, p<0.001, t-test; shorter axis: D-stellate cells, 435.62 ± 1.82 μm, n = 6 cells versus small cells, 148.60 ± 12.03 μm, n = 17, p<0.001, t-test).
source: The small glycinergic cells had significantly restricted branched processes compared with D-stellate cells (longest axis: D-stellate cells, 619.42 ± 45.78 μm versus small cells, 271.43 ± 26.27 μm, p<0.001, t-test; shorter axis: D-stellate cells, 435.62 ± 1.82 μm, n = 6 cells versus small cells, 148.60 ± 12.03 μm, n = 17, p<0.001, t-test) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative morphological measurements.

claim: The field encompassed by D-stellate cell processes had a larger volume and surface area than that of small glycinergic cells.
source: We also measured the volume and surface area under the axonal-dendritic field assessed by its convex hull, and found that the field encompassed by D-stellate cell processes had a larger volume and surface area than that of small glycinergic cells (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative morphological measurements shown in Figures 5E and F.

claim: The small cells showed significantly higher axonal-dendritic arborization closer to their somata as compared with large D-stellate cells (Sholl analysis, p=0.006, K-S test).
source: Moreover, the small cells showed significantly higher axonal-dendritic arborization closer to their somata as compared with large D-stellate cells (Sholl analysis, p=0.006, K-S test) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sholl analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Small glycinergic cells are anatomically distinct from D-stellate cell types.
source: Our morphological data indicate that smaller glycinergic cells are anatomically distinct from D-stellate cell types and provide further evidence that small glycinergic cells are a distinct class of inhibitory neuron.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple morphological measurements.

claim: Small glycinergic cells have a similar spread of the axonal-dendritic field in the longest axis but significantly larger spread in the shortest axis compared to T-stellate cells (longest axis: T-stellate cells, 237.03 ± 16.67 μm versus small cells, 271.43 ± 26.27 μm, p=0.33, t-test; shorter axis: T-stellate cells, 79.73 ± 13.68 μm versus small cells, 148.60 ± 12.03 μm, p<0.005, t-test).
source: Finally, we compared the morphology of small glycinergic cells with excitatory T-stellate (planar) cells, defined as non-GFP containing, dendritic neurons with chopper firing properties (Figure 5C). We found that small glycinergic cells have a similar spread of the axonal-dendritic field in the longest axis but significantly larger spread in the shortest axis (longest axis: T-stellate cells, 237.03 ± 16.67 μm versus small cells, 271.43 ± 26.27 μm, p=0.33, t-test; shorter axis: T-stellate cells, 79.73 ± 13.68 μm versus small cells, 148.60 ± 12.03 μm, p<0.005, t-test) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative morphological measurements comparing small cells to T-stellate cells.

claim: Small glycinergic cells are less planar than T-stellate cells.
source: This suggests that small glycinergic cells are less planar than T-stellate cells.
evidence: This inference is based on the morphological measurements showing larger spread in the shorter axis.

claim: Small glycinergic cells had more profusely branched arbors near their soma whereas T-stellate cells exhibited more branching at the end of dendrites.
source: We also found that small glycinergic cells had more profusely branched arbors near their soma whereas T-stellate cells exhibited more branching at the end of dendrites, which is consistent with the previous studies (Rhode et al., 1983a; Oertel et al., 1990; Figure 5G, Sholl analysis, p<0.05, K-S test).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sholl analysis shown in Figure 5G and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: Small glycinergic cells are morphologically a distinct class of neuron in the VCN.
source: These data confirm that small glycinergic cells are morphologically a distinct class of neuron in the VCN.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple morphological comparisons.

claim: All glycinergic cells showed sustained firing responses at weak-to-moderate depolarizing current steps.
source: All cells showed sustained firing responses at weak-to-moderate depolarizing current steps; however, their responses to strong depolarizing current injections were more diverse (Figure 6A–B, top), particularly as regards the maintenance of spike amplitude during the response.
evidence: This observation is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 6A-B.

claim: Glycinergic cells' responses to strong depolarizing current injections were more diverse, particularly as regards the maintenance of spike amplitude during the response.
source: All cells showed sustained firing responses at weak-to-moderate depolarizing current steps; however, their responses to strong depolarizing current injections were more diverse (Figure 6A–B, top), particularly as regards the maintenance of spike amplitude during the response.
evidence: This observation is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 6A-B.

claim: The elbow method for estimating the optimal number of clusters indicated the presence of two to three groupings of glycinergic cells.
source: The elbow method for estimating the optimal number of clusters (Figure 6G, inset) indicated the presence of two to three groupings of these cells.
evidence: This claim is based on cluster analysis shown in Figure 6G inset.

claim: Cluster analysis based on electrophysiology accurately separated 91.7% (11/12) of visually-identified D-stellate cells from small cells.
source: Cluster analysis based on electrophysiology accurately separated 91.7% (11/12) of visually-identified D-stellate cells (red circles) from small cells (blue).
evidence: This claim is supported by K-means cluster analysis of electrophysiological parameters.

claim: The parameters used to classify the small cells were widely distributed which suggests there may be further subtypes among the small glycinergic cells.
source: However, the parameters used to classify the small cells were widely distributed which suggests there may be further subtypes among the small glycinergic cells.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the distribution of electrophysiological parameters.

claim: The high accuracy of the cluster method for classifying glycinergic cells suggest that small cell types may be solely identified based on the physiological membrane properties of the cells.
source: The high accuracy of the cluster method for classifying glycinergic cells suggest that small cell types may be solely identified based on the physiological membrane properties of the cells.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the cluster analysis results.

claim: Small glycinergic cells can generate 'sustained' chopper responses similar to those seen in vivo.
source: To test whether small cells have the capacity to generate such chopping responses, we recorded from the cells in vitro and applied repeated long depolarizing current steps (200 pA) (Figure 7A). The resulting peristimulus time histograms exhibited features that closely resembled in vivo 'sustained' chopper responses—with well-timed onset action potentials, and subsequent spikes which increasingly accumulated more temporal jitter throughout the duration of the current step, despite little to no adaptation in firing rate (Figure 7B–D, n = 26).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and analysis shown in Figures 7A-D.

claim: Small glycinergic neurons could give acoustic responses like those of principal cells, and possibly be mistaken for such cells in studies in which no other means for cell identification is used.
source: This feature raises the possibility that these smaller neurons could give acoustic responses like those of principal cells, and possibly be mistaken for such cells in studies in which no other means for cell identification is used.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the chopper firing patterns observed.

claim: AN root stimulation readily led to postsynaptic spikes in small GFP-positive cells that exhibited a chopping pattern similar to that seen with current injection.
source: Trains of shocks applied to the AN root readily led to postsynaptic spikes that exhibited a chopping pattern similar to that seen with current injection, although often with a period of 'extra' spikes after the end of stimulation (Figure 7E–H; 6 of 6 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 7E-H.

claim: AN root stimulation evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) that grew in size with the strength of the shocks.
source: In voltage clamp, AN root stimulation evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) that grew in size with the strength of the shocks (Figure 8A), indicating multiple ANF inputs per postsynaptic cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Each small glycinergic cell receives 3–5 ANF inputs.
source: Varying stimulus strength indicated that each cell receives 3–5 ANF inputs (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of graded EPSC amplitudes shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The average maximal amplitude of EPSCs evoked with AN root stimulation was 385.7 ± 49.9 pA (n = 22).
source: The average maximal amplitude of EPSCs evoked with AN root stimulation was 385.7 ± 49.9 pA (n = 22).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of EPSC amplitudes.

claim: The EPSCs showed fast kinetics (τ = 0.80 ± 0.07 ms, half-width = 0.91 ± 0.08 ms, n = 22) with short and consistent synaptic delays of less than 1 ms, consistent with monosynaptic transmission.
source: The EPSCs also showed fast kinetics (τ = 0.80 ± 0.07 ms, half-width = 0.91 ± 0.08 ms, n = 22) with short and consistent synaptic delays of less than 1 ms, consistent with the monosynaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of EPSC kinetics and latencies.

claim: In many small cells (45%, 10/22), AN root stimulation evoked EPSCs with distinctly different latencies.
source: In many small cells (45%, 10/22), AN root stimulation evoked EPSCs with distinctly different latencies (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The presence of peaks with different latencies suggests that the small cells also receive polysynaptic excitation from neurons located within the brain slice.
source: The presence of peaks with different latencies suggests that the small cells also receive polysynaptic excitation from neurons located within the brain slice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of EPSCs with different latencies.

claim: Excitatory T-stellate cells have been shown to make local collaterals.
source: Specifically, the first EPSC always had a short synaptic latency consistent with a monosynaptic input (Figure 8B, black arrowheads), but this was often followed by EPSCs two or more ms later (Figure 8B, gray arrowheads). In the VCN, excitatory T-stellate cells have been shown to make local collaterals (Oertel et al., 1990; Ferragamo et al., 1998a) and can provide some local excitation (Cao et al., 2019) whereas bushy cells do not appear to make local collaterals (Smith et al., 1991; Smith et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: T-stellate cells can provide some local excitation.
source: In the VCN, excitatory T-stellate cells have been shown to make local collaterals (Oertel et al., 1990; Ferragamo et al., 1998a) and can provide some local excitation (Cao et al., 2019) whereas bushy cells do not appear to make local collaterals (Smith et al., 1991; Smith et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Bushy cells do not appear to make local collaterals.
source: In the VCN, excitatory T-stellate cells have been shown to make local collaterals (Oertel et al., 1990; Ferragamo et al., 1998a) and can provide some local excitation (Cao et al., 2019) whereas bushy cells do not appear to make local collaterals (Smith et al., 1991; Smith et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: T-stellate cells can be excited by the cholinergic agonist carbachol.
source: Moreover, Fujino and Oertel, 2001 showed that T-stellate cells can be excited by the cholinergic agonist carbachol.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Carbachol application resulted in a significant increase in the amplitude and frequency of sEPSCs in small GFP-positive cells.
source: To test this idea, carbachol (10 μM) was bath applied while monitoring spontaneous EPSCs (sEPSCs) from small GFP-positive cells. We observed a significant increase in the amplitude and frequency of sEPSCs (Figure 8C,D), as expected if the T-stellate cells were firing spontaneously.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 8C-D.

claim: Carbachol application significantly increased the number of delayed EPSCs (short latency events < 1 ms, percentage increase = 17.57 ± 0.11%; longer latency events, percentage increase = 92.00 ± 0.13%).
source: Across multiple cells (n = 5), there was no significant increase in the number of EPSCs with a latency <1 ms (percentage increase from control = 17.57 ± 0.11%). By contrast, we observed a significant increase in the number of events with longer latencies (percentage increase from control = 92.00 ± 0.13%).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EPSC latencies before and after carbachol application.

claim: The local collaterals from T-stellates are the source of polysynaptic excitatory inputs onto the small glycinergic cells.
source: These results strongly suggest that the local collaterals from T-stellates are the source of polysynaptic excitatory inputs onto the small glycinergic cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the carbachol experiments showing selective increase in delayed EPSCs.

claim: D-stellate cells project into DCN.
source: Next, we examined the projections of the small GFP-positive neurons. D-stellate cells project into DCN (Smith and Rhode, 1989; Oertel et al., 2011), as well as to the contralateral CN (Wenthold, 1987; Shore et al., 1992; Schofield and Cant, 1996b; Alibardi, 1998; Doucet et al., 1999; Needham and Paolini, 2003; Doucet and Ryugo, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: D-stellate cells project to the contralateral CN.
source: Next, we examined the projections of the small GFP-positive neurons. D-stellate cells project into DCN (Smith and Rhode, 1989; Oertel et al., 2011), as well as to the contralateral CN (Wenthold, 1987; Shore et al., 1992; Schofield and Cant, 1996b; Alibardi, 1998; Doucet et al., 1999; Needham and Paolini, 2003; Doucet and Ryugo, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Some GFP positive neurons were double-labeled with retrobeads in contralateral CN, however, virtually all of these had large somas, consistent with D-stellate cells (length of longest axis = 26.91 ± 3.92 μm, n = 47, n = 3 CNs).
source: Some GFP positive neurons were double-labeled with retrobeads in contralateral CN, however, virtually all of these had large somas, consistent with D-stellate cells (length of longest axis = 26.91 ± 3.92 μm, n = 47, n = 3 CNs) (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrobead tracing experiments shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Few if any of the small GFP-positive cells project contralaterally.
source: Thus, few if any of the small GFP-positive cells project contralaterally, again indicating that they compose a separate cell class.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the retrobead tracing experiments showing only large cells were labeled.

claim: A subset (9/15) of the small GFP-positive cells can be activated by bath application of carbachol (10 μM).
source: Interestingly, we have found that a subset (9/15) of the small GFP-positive cells can be activated by bath application of carbachol (10 μM; n = 15; Figure 10A).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Carbachol sensitive and insensitive small cells did not differ in intrinsic properties.
source: Carbachol sensitive and insensitive small cells did not differ in intrinsic properties (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of intrinsic properties shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: D-stellate cells failed to respond to carbachol.
source: By contrast, the other major inhibitory sources to VCN, including the D-stellate (n = 6) (Figure 10B) and the tubercoluventral cells of the DCN (n = 5) (Figure 10C), failed to respond to carbachol.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Tuberculoventral cells of the DCN failed to respond to carbachol.
source: By contrast, the other major inhibitory sources to VCN, including the D-stellate (n = 6) (Figure 10B) and the tubercoluventral cells of the DCN (n = 5) (Figure 10C), failed to respond to carbachol.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The lack of carbachol sensitivity in the D-stellate cells is consistent with observations reported by Fujino and Oertel, 2001.
source: This lack of carbachol sensitivity in the D-stellate cells is consistent with observations reported by Fujino and Oertel, 2001.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Carbachol application produced a clear increase in the frequency of spontaneous IPSCs (sIPSCs) in both bushy and T-stellate cells (inter-event interval, control = 280.4 ± 47.6 ms versus carbachol = 191.2 ± 29.0 ms, p<0.02, t-test, n = 18).
source: Carbachol application produced a clear increase in the frequency of spontaneous IPSCs (sIPSCs) in both bushy and T-stellate cells (Figure 10D and E) (inter-event interval, control = 280.4 ± 47.6 ms versus carbachol = 191.2 ± 29.0 ms, p<0.02, t-test, n = 18) (Figure 10J).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 10D-E and quantified in Figure 10J.

claim: The decay time course of the sIPSCs was consistent with cell-specific kinetics reported previously (bushy cell, τ = 7.22 ± 1.40 ms, n = 9, T-stellate, τ = 2.28 ± 0.07 ms, n = 9).
source: The decay time course of the sIPSCs (bushy cell, τ = 7.22 ± 1.40 ms, n = 9, T-stellate, τ = 2.28 ± 0.07 ms, n = 9) (Figure 10F–I), consistent with cell-specific kinetics reported previously (Xie and Manis, 2013a; Xie and Manis, 2014; Lin and Xie, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of IPSC kinetics and citations to prior studies.

claim: The small GFP-positive, glycinergic cells likely act as local interneurons.
source: Thus, the small GFP-positive, glycinergic cells likely act as local interneurons.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the carbachol experiments showing increased IPSCs in principal cells.

claim: L-stellate cells are molecularly, anatomically, and electrophysiologically distinct from the well-studied, D-stellate cell types.
source: This study used transgenic animals, combined with molecular, morphological, and electrophysiological techniques to show that the L-stellate cells are molecularly, anatomically, and electrophysiologically distinct from the well-studied, D-stellate cell types.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by multiple lines of evidence.

claim: L-stellate cells constitute the vast majority of glycinergic cells in the VCN.
source: Moreover, L-stellate cells constitute the vast majority of glycinergic cells in the VCN.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell counting data.

claim: L-stellate cells receive monosynaptic AN inputs and feedforward excitatory inputs from local T-stellate cells.
source: They receive monosynaptic AN inputs and feedforward excitatory inputs from local T-stellate cells, and their axons appear to inhibit principal excitatory cells, bushy cells, and T-stellate cells of the VCN (Figure 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and is summarized in Figure 11.

claim: L-stellate cell axons appear to inhibit principal excitatory cells, bushy cells, and T-stellate cells of the VCN.
source: They receive monosynaptic AN inputs and feedforward excitatory inputs from local T-stellate cells, and their axons appear to inhibit principal excitatory cells, bushy cells, and T-stellate cells of the VCN (Figure 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and is summarized in Figure 11.

claim: The VCN has a distinct population of glycinergic interneurons that likely play a unique role in auditory processing.
source: Therefore, the VCN has a distinct population of glycinergic interneurons that likely play a unique role in auditory processing.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Complex arrays of inhibitory interneurons sculpt the responses of excitatory neurons and dynamically regulate the local circuity across brain regions.
source: Across brain regions, complex arrays of inhibitory interneurons sculpt the responses of excitatory neurons and dynamically regulate the local circuity.
evidence: This is general knowledge about brain circuitry.

claim: Diverse inhibitory cell types would be anticipated to exist in the VCN, one of the first stations of auditory signal processing.
source: Therefore, diverse inhibitory cell types would be anticipated to exist in the VCN, one of the first stations of auditory signal processing.
evidence: This is an inference based on general principles of brain organization.

claim: Previous staining and reconstruction studies have hinted at additional small, potentially local glycinergic neurons.
source: Although previous staining and reconstruction studies have hinted at additional small, potentially local glycinergic neurons (Lorente de Nó, 1981; Wenthold, 1987; Kolston et al., 1992; Doucet and Ryugo, 1997; Gleich and Vater, 1998; Doucet et al., 1999), it has been a challenge to identify such cells based only on morphological and electrophysiological features.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: It has been a challenge to identify small glycinergic cells based only on morphological and electrophysiological features.
source: Although previous staining and reconstruction studies have hinted at additional small, potentially local glycinergic neurons (Lorente de Nó, 1981; Wenthold, 1987; Kolston et al., 1992; Doucet and Ryugo, 1997; Gleich and Vater, 1998; Doucet et al., 1999), it has been a challenge to identify such cells based only on morphological and electrophysiological features.
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges in the field.

claim: Due to their size, small cells are generally not targeted well for cell-filling procedures, especially in vivo.
source: Due to their size, small cells are generally not targeted well for cell-filling procedures, especially in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about technical challenges in studying small cells.

claim: Electrophysiologically, the glycinergic L-stellate cells fire regularly, similar to excitatory T-stellate cells.
source: Electrophysiologically, the glycinergic L-stellate cells fire regularly, similar to excitatory T-stellate cells (Oertel, 1983; Rhode et al., 1983b; Young et al., 1988; Oertel et al., 2011), and thus could have occasionally been mistaken for T-stellate cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and citations to prior studies.

claim: L-stellate cells could have occasionally been mistaken for T-stellate cells in prior studies.
source: Electrophysiologically, the glycinergic L-stellate cells fire regularly, similar to excitatory T-stellate cells (Oertel, 1983; Rhode et al., 1983b; Young et al., 1988; Oertel et al., 2011), and thus could have occasionally been mistaken for T-stellate cells.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the similarity in firing patterns.

claim: Morphological and electrophysiological features provide an initial platform for further classification of interneurons.
source: Morphological and electrophysiological features provide an initial platform for further classification of interneurons.
evidence: This is a general statement about approaches to cell classification.

claim: When morphological and electrophysiological approaches are applied to transgenic animals expressing different molecular markers in inhibitory cell types, a clearer systematic classification system can emerge.
source: When these approaches are applied to transgenic animals expressing different molecular markers in inhibitory cell types, a clearer systematic classification system can emerge (Wonders and Anderson, 2006; Cadwell et al., 2016; Fuzik et al., 2016; Tremblay et al., 2016; Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on cell classification.

claim: Further studies may reveal additional diversity within the L-stellate and D-stellate cell groups.
source: Although we have identified two major glycinergic interneuron populations, further studies may reveal additional diversity within the groups described in this paper.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Anatomical data show a variety of somatic, dendritic, and axonal morphologies within the L-stellate cell types.
source: Our anatomical data show a variety of somatic, dendritic, and axonal morphologies within the L-stellate cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological reconstructions.

claim: L-stellate cell types display heterogeneity in their membrane properties, likely a consequence of diverse ion channel expression.
source: Electrophysiologically, L-stellate cell types display heterogeneity in their membrane properties, likely a consequence of diverse ion channel expression.
evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiological measurements and inference about ion channels.

claim: Only a subset of L-stellate cells was sensitive to the cholinergic agonist, carbachol.
source: We also found that only a subset of L-stellate cells was sensitive to the cholinergic agonist, carbachol.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Medial olivocochlear axons may make synaptic contacts with T-stellate cells and small unidentified cells in the VCN.
source: Previous studies have reported that medial olivocochlear axons may make synaptic contacts with T-stellate cells and small unidentified cells in the VCN (Benson and Brown, 1990; Benson et al., 1996; Fujino and Oertel, 2001; Oertel and Fujino, 2001; Mellott et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A substantial cholinergic input into CN is reported from the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPT) and the latero-dorsal tegmental nucleus (LDT).
source: In addition to major cholinergic projections from the superior olivary complex, a substantial cholinergic input into CN is also reported from the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PPT) and the latero-dorsal tegmental nucleus (LDT) (Mellott et al., 2011; Schofield et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Cholinergic inputs to CN have been proposed to improve frequency selectivity, improve sound detection, or improve speech in noisy backgrounds.
source: Cholinergic inputs to CN have been proposed to improve frequency selectivity, improve sound detection, or improve speech in noisy backgrounds (Winslow and Sachs, 1987; Winslow and Sachs, 1988; Kawase et al., 1993; Fujino and Oertel, 2001; Mulders et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Some L-stellate cells may receive inputs from cholinergic sources.
source: As some L-stellate cells were activated by bath application of carbachol, this suggests that the L-stellate cells might also receive inputs from cholinergic sources.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the carbachol sensitivity of some L-stellate cells.

claim: L-cells may provide feedforward inhibition to control the excitability of T-stellate cells and bushy cells thereby regulating the signal detection in a noisy background.
source: L-cells may provide feedforward inhibition to control the excitability of T-stellate cells and bushy cells thereby regulating the signal detection in a noisy background.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional role of L-stellate cells.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis will likely allow further definition of subpopulations of glycinergic interneurons in the VCN.
source: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis will likely allow further definition of subpopulations of glycinergic interneurons in the VCN (Jiang et al., 2015; Cadwell et al., 2016; Fuzik et al., 2016; Shrestha et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions supported by citations to prior transcriptomic studies.

claim: L-stellate cells had smaller soma sizes and exhibited tightly branched axons and dendrites compared to D-stellate cells.
source: In comparison to D-stellate cells, L-stellate cells had smaller soma sizes and exhibited tightly branched axons and dendrites.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological measurements.

claim: The restricted dendritic and axonal processes of L-stellate cells suggest that they have narrow frequency-band receptive fields.
source: These restricted dendritic and axonal processes suggest that L-stellate cells have narrow frequency-band receptive fields.
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphological characteristics of L-stellate cells.

claim: D-stellate cells have been termed the 'wide-band inhibitor'.
source: This morphology is very different from the D-stellate cell, which has been termed the 'wide-band inhibitor' (Nelken and Young, 1994; Arnott et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The potential for narrow band excitation of the L-stellate cells could provide a means for inhibition to excitatory cells in nearby isofrequency lamina in VCN.
source: The potential for narrow band excitation of the L-stellate cells could provide a means for inhibition to excitatory cells in nearby isofrequency lamina in VCN.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional role of L-stellate cells.

claim: Inhibition has been proposed to improve tuning properties and temporal precision, and stabilizes neuronal firing responses to acoustic inputs.
source: Inhibition has been proposed to improve tuning properties and temporal precision, and stabilizes neuronal firing responses to acoustic inputs (Gai and Carney, 2008; Keine and Rübsamen, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The majority of local inhibitory inputs onto excitatory neurons could originate from L-stellate cells.
source: Indeed, as the D-stellate cells are numerically a minority of the glycinergic VCN cell population compared to the L-stellate cells, we propose that the majority of local inhibitory inputs onto excitatory neurons could originate from L-stellate cells.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the numerical abundance of L-stellate cells.

claim: The commissural D-stellate cell connects ipsi- and contralateral CN.
source: The commissural D-stellate cell connects ipsi- and contralateral CN.
evidence: This is established knowledge about D-stellate cell projections.

claim: Previous tract tracing studies in rat reported a presence of small commissural glycinergic cells.
source: Previous tract tracing studies in rat reported a presence of small commissural glycinergic cells (Doucet and Ryugo, 2006), but we did not observe any L-stellate cells retrogradely labelled in our mouse study, consistent with a locally restricted axonal arbor.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study and contrasted with the current findings.

claim: It remains possible that some L-stellate cells also project outside the VCN, perhaps to the ipsilateral DCN or the granule cell region.
source: However, our cell-filling experiments only sampled a subset of cells, and it remains possible that some L-stellate cells also project outside the VCN, perhaps to the ipsilateral DCN or the granule cell region.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging limitations of the study.

claim: Many L-stellate cells were located near the margins of VCN, near granule cell regions.
source: Indeed, many L-stellate cells were located near the margins of VCN, near granule cell regions.
evidence: This observation is based on imaging data.

claim: Some L-stellate cells could be the small multipolar marginal cells described by Doucet and Ryugo, 2006.
source: These could be the small multipolar marginal cells described by Doucet and Ryugo, 2006.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the location of L-stellate cells.

claim: It is possible that some L-stellate cells were Golgi cells.
source: As inhibitory Golgi cells are located in and near the granule cell layer (Mugnaini et al., 1980; Ferragamo et al., 1998b; Irie et al., 2006; Yaeger and Trussell, 2015), it is possible that some L-stellate cells were Golgi cells.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the location of L-stellate cells and citations to prior studies on Golgi cells.

claim: VCN receives projecting glycinergic inputs from the tuberculoventral cells of the DCN.
source: In addition to local glycinergic sources, VCN receives projecting glycinergic inputs from the tuberculoventral cells of the DCN (Wickesberg and Oertel, 1988; Wickesberg and Oertel, 1990; Wickesberg et al., 1991; Xie and Manis, 2013a; Campagnola and Manis, 2014; Muniak and Ryugo, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Tuberculoventral cells have narrow frequency-receptive fields and project to a tonotopically matched region in the VCN.
source: Tuberculoventral cells have narrow frequency-receptive fields and project to a tonotopically matched region in the VCN.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tuberculoventral cells.

claim: Tuberculoventral cells have been proposed to provide narrow band inhibition.
source: Therefore, tuberculoventral cells have been proposed to provide narrow band inhibition, but at present, it is unclear whether the local glycinergic inputs from L-stellate cells and the long-range inputs from tuberculoventral cells play different roles in sculpting the responses of the excitatory VCN neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about a proposed function of tuberculoventral cells.

claim: It is unclear whether the local glycinergic inputs from L-stellate cells and the long-range inputs from tuberculoventral cells play different roles in sculpting the responses of the excitatory VCN neurons.
source: Therefore, tuberculoventral cells have been proposed to provide narrow band inhibition, but at present, it is unclear whether the local glycinergic inputs from L-stellate cells and the long-range inputs from tuberculoventral cells play different roles in sculpting the responses of the excitatory VCN neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about an open question in the field.

claim: VCN principal cells could receive input from both L-stellate cells and tuberculoventral cells.
source: Conceivably, VCN principal cells could receive input from both subtypes of interneuron, and the differential activation and modulation of those interneurons could aid in fine tuning auditory processing under different conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about potential circuit organization.

claim: The differential activation and modulation of L-stellate cells and tuberculoventral cells could aid in fine tuning auditory processing under different conditions.
source: Conceivably, VCN principal cells could receive input from both subtypes of interneuron, and the differential activation and modulation of those interneurons could aid in fine tuning auditory processing under different conditions.
